questions.q:
The heat extracted out of $x$ gram of water initially at $50°C$ to cool it down to $0°C$ is sufficient to evaporate $(1000 - x)$ gram of water also initially at $50°C$. The value of $x$ (closest integer) is _______.
(Take latent heat of water $2256\text{ kJ/kg.K}$, specific heat capacity of water $4200\text{ J/kg.K}$)
questions.solution:
Heat extracted to cool $x$ gram of water from $50^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ is given by:

$Q_1 = m_1 c \Delta T_1$

$Q_1 = x \times 4.2 \times (50 - 0) = 210x \text{ J}$

Heat required to raise the temperature of $(1000 - x)$ gram of water from $50^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ and evaporate it is given by:

$Q_2 = m_2 c \Delta T_2 + m_2 L$

$Q_2 = (1000 - x) \times [4.2 \times (100 - 50) + 2256]$

$Q_2 = (1000 - x) \times (210 + 2256) = 2466(1000 - x) \text{ J}$

Equating the heat extracted and the heat required:

$Q_1 = Q_2$

$210x = 2466(1000 - x)$

$210x = 2466000 - 2466x$

$2676x = 2466000$

$x = \dfrac{2466000}{2676} \approx 921.52$

The closest integer value for $x$ is $922$.

Answer: $922$

questions.q: The temperature of a metal strip having coefficient of linear expansion $\alpha$ is increased from $T_1$ to $T_2$ resulting in increase of its length by $\Delta L_1$. The temperature is further increased from $T_2$ to $T_3$ such that the increase in its length is $\Delta L_2$. Given $T_3+T_1=2T_2$ and $T_2-T_1=\Delta T$, the value of $\Delta L_2$ is ______.
questions.solution:
Let the length of the metal strip at temperature $T_1$ be $L_1$.

When the temperature is increased from $T_1$ to $T_2$, the new length $L_2$ is given by:

$L_2 = L_1(1 + \alpha \Delta T)$

where $\Delta T = T_2 - T_1$.

The increase in length is:

$\Delta L_1 = L_2 - L_1 = L_1 \alpha \Delta T$

When the temperature is further increased from $T_2$ to $T_3$, the new length $L_3$ is:

$L_3 = L_2(1 + \alpha \Delta T')$

where $\Delta T' = T_3 - T_2$.

Given $T_3 + T_1 = 2T_2$, we have $T_3 - T_2 = T_2 - T_1 = \Delta T$.

Thus, $\Delta T' = \Delta T$.

The increase in length for this second temperature change is:

$\Delta L_2 = L_3 - L_2 = L_2 \alpha \Delta T$

Substituting $L_2 = L_1(1 + \alpha \Delta T)$ into the equation for $\Delta L_2$:

$\Delta L_2 = L_1(1 + \alpha \Delta T) \alpha \Delta T$

$\Delta L_2 = (L_1 \alpha \Delta T)(1 + \alpha \Delta T)$

Since $\Delta L_1 = L_1 \alpha \Delta T$, substituting this gives:

$\Delta L_2 = \Delta L_1(1 + \alpha \Delta T)$

Answer: $\Delta L_1[1+\alpha\Delta T]$

10 kg of ice at $-10^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is added to 100 kg of water to lower its temperature from 25 ${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Consider no heat exchange to surroundings. The decrement to the temperature of water is $\_\_\_\_${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
(specific heat of ice $=2100 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{Kg}.{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, specific heat of water $=4200 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{Kg}.{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, latent heat of fusion of ice $=3.36 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{Kg}$)
questions.solution:
Heat available from water cooling 25°C to 0°C: $Q_{available} = 100 \times 4200 \times 25 = 10.5 \times 10^6$ J.
Heat to warm ice from -10°C to 0°C: $Q_1 = 10 \times 2100 \times 10 = 0.21 \times 10^6$ J.
Heat to melt ice at 0°C: $Q_2 = 10 \times 3.36 \times 10^5 = 3.36 \times 10^6$ J.
Total needed: $0.21 + 3.36 = 3.57 \times 10^6$ J.
Since available heat exceeds required heat, all ice melts. Remaining heat: $10.5 - 3.57 = 6.93 \times 10^6$ J
warms 110 kg water: $\Delta T = \frac{6.93 \times 10^6}{110 \times 4200} = 15$ °C.
Final temperature: 15°C.
Decrement in water temperature: $25 - 15 = 10$ °C.

questions.q: A brass wire of length 2 m and radius 1 mm at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is held taut between two rigid supports. Initially it was cooled to a temperature of $-43^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ creating a tension $T$ in the wire. The temperature to which the wire has to be cooled in order to increase the tension in it to $1.4 T$, is $\_\_\_\_${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.
questions.solution:
Thermal stress in the wire is caused by contraction.
At -43°C, the temperature drop from 27°C is $\Delta T_1 = 70°C$
It creates tension $T = YA\alpha\Delta T_1$ where $Y$ is Young's modulus and $\alpha$ is linear expansion coefficient.
For tension to increase to $1.4T$, the new temperature drop must be: $\Delta T_2 = 1.4 \times 70 = 98°C$.
Required temperature: $T_3 = 27 - 98 = -71°C$

A gas based geyser heats water flowing at the rate of 5.0 litres per minute from $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $87^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The rate of consumption of the gas is $\_\_\_\_$\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{s}$.
(Take heat of combustion of gas $=5.0 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{g}$) specific heat capacity of water $=4200 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{kg} \cdot{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$
questions.solution:
Flow rate = 5.0 L/min = 5.0 kg/min, $\Delta T = 87 - 27 = 60$°C
Heat required per minute: $Q = mc\Delta T = 5.0 \times 4200 \times 60 = 1.26 \times 10^6$ J/min
If m grams of gas consumed per minute:
$m \times 5.0 \times 10^4 = 1.26 \times 10^6$
$m = \frac{1.26 \times 10^6}{5.0 \times 10^4} = 25.2$ g/min
Rate $= \frac{25.2}{60} = 0.42$ g/s

questions.q:
Two cylindrical rods A and B made of different materials, are joined in a straight line. The ratio of lengths, radii and thermal conductivities of these rods are :
$\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{1}{2}, \frac{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{B}}}=2$ and $\frac{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{1}{2}$. The free ends of rods A and B are maintained at $400 \mathrm{~K}, 200 \mathrm{~K}$, respectively. The temperature of rods interface is ________ K, when equilibrium is established.
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{R}_1=\frac{\ell_1}{\mathrm{~K}_1 \mathrm{~A}_1}, \mathrm{R}_2=\frac{\ell_2}{\mathrm{~K}_2 \mathrm{~A}_2} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{dQ}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{T}}{\mathrm{R}} \\ & \left(\frac{\mathrm{dQ}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right)_1=\left(\frac{\mathrm{dQ}}{\mu}\right)_2 \\ & \frac{400-\mathrm{T}}{\mathrm{R}_1}=\frac{\mathrm{T}-200}{\mathrm{R}_2} \\ & \frac{400-\mathrm{T}}{\mathrm{T}-200}=\frac{\mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{R}_2}=\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_2}{\mathrm{r}_1}\right)^2 \times \frac{\mathrm{K}_2}{\mathrm{~K}_1} \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \times\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 \times 2 \\ & =\left(\frac{1}{4}\right) \\ & \frac{400-\mathrm{T}}{\mathrm{T}-200}=\frac{1}{4} \\ & 1600-4 \mathrm{~T}=\mathrm{T}-200 \\ & 5 \mathrm{~T}=1800 \\ & \mathrm{~T}=360 \mathrm{~K}\end{aligned}$

(Given $\sigma=6.0 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~W} \mathrm{~m}^{-2} \mathrm{~K}^{-4}, \pi=3.14$ and assume that the emissivity of wire material is same at all wavelength.)
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{L}=10 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{~d}=0.5 \mathrm{~mm}, \mathrm{~T}=1727^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=2000 \mathrm{~K}$
Power, $\mathrm{P}=94.2 \mathrm{~W}$

$94.2=\varepsilon \times\left(6 \times 10^{-8}\right)(3.14)(0.5)\left(10^{-3}\right)$
$\left(10 \times 10^{-2}\right)(2000)^4$
$\varepsilon=\frac{94.2}{(94.2)(16)}=\frac{5}{8}$

questions.q: Two conductors have the same resistances at $0 ° C$ but their temperature coefficients of resistance are ${\alpha}_{1}$ and ${\alpha}_{2}$. The respective temperature coefficients for their series and parallel combinations are :
questions.solution:
Change in resistance due to temperature is given by, ${R}^{'} = R\left(1 + \alpha ∆ T\right)$

For Series Combination:

${R}_{eq} = {R}_{1} + {R}_{2}$

$⇒ 2R\left(1 + {\alpha}_{eq} ∆ T\right) = R\left(1 + {\alpha}_{1} ∆ T\right) + R\left(1 + {\alpha}_{2} ∆ T\right)$

$⇒ 2R\left(1 + {\alpha}_{eq} ∆ T\right) = 2R + \left({\alpha}_{1} + {\alpha}_{2}\right)R ∆ T$

$⇒ {\alpha}_{eq} = \dfrac{{\alpha}_{1} + {\alpha}_{2}}{2}$

For Parallel Combination:

$\dfrac{1}{{R}_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{{R}_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{{R}_{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{R}{2}\left(1 + {\alpha}_{eq} ∆ T\right)} = \dfrac{1}{R\left(1 + {\alpha}_{1} ∆ T\right)} + \dfrac{1}{R\left(1 + {\alpha}_{2} ∆ T\right)}$

$⇒ \dfrac{2}{1 + {\alpha}_{eq} ∆ T} = \dfrac{1}{1 + {\alpha}_{1} ∆ T} + \dfrac{1}{1 + {\alpha}_{2} ∆ T}$

$⇒ \dfrac{2}{1 + {\alpha}_{eq} ∆ T} = \dfrac{1 + {\alpha}_{2} ∆ T + 1 + {\alpha}_{1} ∆ T}{\left(1 + {\alpha}_{1} ∆ T\right)\left(1 + {\alpha}_{2} ∆ T\right)}$

$⇒ 2\left[\left(1 + {\alpha}_{1} ∆ T\right)\left(1 + {\alpha}_{2} ∆ T\right)\right] = \left[2 + \left({\alpha}_{1} + {\alpha}_{2}\right) ∆ T\right]\left[1 + {\alpha}_{eq} ∆ T\right]$

$⇒ 2\left[1 + {\alpha}_{1} ∆ T + {\alpha}_{2} ∆ T + {\alpha}_{1}{\alpha}_{2} ∆ T\right] = 2 + 2{\alpha}_{eq} ∆ T + \left({\alpha}_{1} + {\alpha}_{2}\right) ∆ T + {\alpha}_{eq}\left({\alpha}_{1} + {\alpha}_{2}\right) ∆ {T}^{2}$

Neglecting small terms

$2 + 2\left({\alpha}_{1} + {\alpha}_{2}\right) ∆ T = 2 + 2{\alpha}_{eq} ∆ T + \left({\alpha}_{1} + {\alpha}_{2}\right) ∆ T$

$⇒ \left({\alpha}_{1} + {\alpha}_{2}\right) ∆ T = 2{\alpha}_{eq} ∆ T$

$⇒ {\alpha}_{eq} = \dfrac{{\alpha}_{1} + {\alpha}_{2}}{2}$

questions.q: A block of ice at $- 10 ° C$ is slowly heated and converted to steam at $100 ° C$. Which of the following curves represent the phenomenon qualitatively:
questions.solution:
When the state of the substance is not changing, temperature of the substance increases when heat is supplied to it. But when the substance changes the state, the heat supplied to it used as latent heat and the temperature remains constant until all the substance converts to other state.

Therefore, temperature of ice first increases from  $- 10 ° C$ to $0 ° C$. Then, remains constant at $0 ° C$ till whole ice is melted. Then, it increases from $0 ° C$ to $100 ° C$. Again it remains constant at $100 ° C$ till whole water converts into steam.

questions.q: A body cools from ${80}^{o}C$ to ${60}^{o}$ in $5$ minutes. The temperature for the surrounding is ${20}^{o}C$. The time it takes to cool from ${60}^{o}C$ to ${40}^{o}C$ is
questions.solution:
The formula to calculate the rate of cooling of the object is given by

$\dfrac{dT}{dt} = K\left[\dfrac{{T}_{f} + {T}_{i}}{2} - {T}_{0}\right] . . . \left(1\right)$

For the first case, it can be written, using equation (1) that

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{80 - 60}{5} & = & K\left[\dfrac{80 + 60}{2} - 20\right] \\ 4 & = & 50K . . . \left(2\right)\end{cases}$

If $t$ is the required time for the second case, from equation (1), it can be written that

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{60 - 40}{t} & = & K\left[\dfrac{60 + 40}{2} - 20\right] \\ \dfrac{20}{t} & = & 30K . . . \left(3\right)\end{cases}$

Divide equation (2) by equation (3) and solve to calculate the required time.

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{4}{\dfrac{20}{t}} & = & \dfrac{50K}{30K} \\ & ⇒ & \dfrac{t}{5} = \dfrac{5}{3} \\ & ⇒ & t = \dfrac{25}{3}min = 500s\end{cases}$

The work to be done in the process is given by

Heat provided to water will be responsible for increase in temperature. Therefore, we can write

$η \times P \times t = M \times s \times \DeltaT$

$v = 500m{s}^{- 1}$

$= \dfrac{4 . 2}{6} \times {10}^{- 3} = 0 . 7 \times {10}^{- 3}kg{sec}^{- 1}$

$= 42g{min}^{- 1}$

questions.solution:
If we heat-up an object, then, the energy is used to either change the temperature of the body or to change the state of the body.
If it changes the temperature, then,

$Q = mS ∆ T$
where, $Q$ is the heat given, $m$ is the mass and $∆ T$ is the change in temperature.

We know that a moving object has an energy in the form of kinetic energy, i.e.,
$KE = \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}$

When that moving object strikes another object, it loses some energy which changes into the heat energy and this heat energy increases the temperature of the object.

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{4} ( 2700 ) = ( 100 ) ( 0 . 42 ) ( ∆ T )$
$⇒ ∆ T = 16 . 07 ° C$

The thermal conductivity of the material of the inner cylinder is ${K}_{1}$ and that of the outer cylinder is ${K}_{2}$. $q = {q}_{1} + {q}_{2}$

$q = \dfrac{K . {\left(2R\right)}^{2}}{l} . \DeltaT$

On comparison,

$K = \dfrac{{K}_{1} + 3{K}_{2}}{4}$.

Let $\left({\theta}^{4} - {\theta}_{0}^{4}\right) = x$

$4{\theta}^{3}d\theta = dx$

$∫ \dfrac{dx}{4x} = - \dfrac{\sigmaAe}{M\alpha}{\left[t\right]}_{0}^{t}$

$\dfrac{1}{4}\left[lnx\right] = \dfrac{M\sigmaAe}{M\alpha}{\left[t\right]}_{0}^{t}$

$t = \dfrac{\alphaM}{16\pi\sigma{R}^{2}}ln\left(\dfrac{16}{3}\right)$

questions.q: If a piece of metal is heated to temperature$\theta$ and then allowed to cool in a room which is at temperature${\theta}_{0}$, the graph between the temperature $T$ of the metal and time $t$ will be closest to :
questions.solution:
According to Newton's cooling law, rate of cooling is

$\dfrac{d \theta}{d t} ∝ \left(\theta - {\theta}_{0}\right)$

Here, $\theta =$the temperature of the body

${\theta}_{0} =$Room temperature(constant)

Let $k$ be the proportionality constant and ${\theta}_{i}$ be the initial temperature.
Therefore,

$\dfrac{d \theta}{d t} = - k\left(\theta - {\theta}_{0}\right) ⇒ ∫ \dfrac{d \theta}{\left(\theta - {\theta}_{0}\right)} = - k ∫ d t ⇒ ln\left(\theta - {\theta}_{0}\right) = - kt ⇒ \theta = {\theta}_{0} + \left(\theta - {\theta}_{0}\right){e}^{- kt}$

Hence, the graph is exponential.
